titlePl: Matura PR: Żywienie — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Food — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Żywienie na maturę rozszerzoną: dieta, przemysł spożywczy i jedzenie poza domem. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended Matura food and nutrition: diet, the food industry and eating out.

items.definitionEn: having a salty or spicy flavour rather than a sweet one
items.example: I prefer a savoury breakfast to cakes and jam.

items.definitionEn: with very little flavour
items.example: Without herbs the soup tastes bland.

items.definitionEn: no longer fresh, especially bread or biscuits
items.example: Throw the stale bread to the birds, not in the bin.

items.definitionEn: likely to go bad quickly if not kept cold
items.example: Put perishable goods in the fridge as soon as you return.

items.definitionEn: having a very strong smell or taste
items.example: Blue cheese has a pungent smell that not everyone likes.

items.definitionEn: having a sharp, pleasant taste, often of citrus or yoghurt
items.example: The dressing is tangy because of the lemon juice.

items.definitionEn: tender and full of juice
items.example: The peaches were succulent after a week of sun.

items.definitionEn: pleasant enough to eat or drink
items.example: School stew is palatable if you add pepper.

items.definitionEn: unpleasant to eat; hard to accept
items.example: Cold tinned tomatoes are unpalatable on their own.

items.definitionEn: looking or smelling so good that you want to eat it
items.example: The bakery window was full of mouth-watering pastries.

items.definitionEn: making you want to eat because of how it looks or smells
items.example: A colourful salad looks more appetising than grey mash.

items.definitionEn: smelling or tasting unpleasant because fat has gone bad
items.example: The oil in the cupboard had turned rancid.

items.definitionEn: unpleasantly wet and soft
items.example: Nobody wants soggy chips at the end of a long queue.

items.definitionEn: firm and making a sharp sound when you bite
items.example: Add crunchy nuts just before you serve the salad.

items.definitionEn: soft and easy to cut or chew
items.example: Slow cooking made the lamb tender.

items.definitionEn: difficult to chew because the meat is hard
items.example: The steak was too tough to enjoy.

items.definitionEn: meat with little fat
items.example: Choose lean meat if you are watching saturated fat.

items.definitionEn: good for your health; made from simple, decent ingredients
items.example: A wholesome packed lunch beats a chocolate bar.

items.definitionEn: containing substances the body needs to stay healthy
items.example: Lentils are a nutritious source of protein.

items.definitionPl: taki, że chce się jeść więcej
items.definitionEn: so pleasant that you want another mouthful
items.example: Those olives are moreish, so put the jar away.

items.definitionEn: too sweet in an unpleasant way
items.example: The dessert was sickly-sweet after two spoons.

items.definitionEn: very hot, especially of food just served
items.example: Serve the soup piping hot with crusty bread.

items.definitionEn: only slightly warm, often when it should be hotter
items.example: A cup of tepid tea is a disappointing end to breakfast.

items.definitionEn: salt, pepper or spices added to improve flavour
items.example: Taste the stew before you add more seasoning.

items.definitionEn: a small amount of food used to decorate a dish
items.example: A garnish of parsley makes the plate look finished.

items.definitionEn: a sauce or seasoning eaten with food, such as mustard
items.example: Mustard is the condiment I always keep on the table.

items.definitionEn: a flavoured liquid in which you soak food before cooking
items.example: Leave the chicken in the marinade overnight.

items.definitionEn: dried seeds such as beans, lentils and peas used as food
items.example: Dried pulses are cheap, filling and rich in protein.

items.definitionEn: a basic food that a population eats regularly
items.example: Bread is still a staple food in many European homes.

items.definitionEn: made from the complete grain, not only the refined part
items.example: A bowl of wholegrain pasta keeps you full for longer.

items.definitionEn: a type of fat, often from animals, that should be eaten in limited amounts
items.example: Butter is high in saturated fat.

items.definitionEn: the part of plants that helps digestion and is not fully absorbed
items.example: Oats and beans are rich in dietary fibre.

items.definitionEn: a substance added to food to colour, preserve or flavour it
items.example: Read the label if you want to avoid a controversial additive.

items.definitionEn: a substance added so that food lasts longer
items.example: Some juices use lemon juice as a natural preservative.

items.definitionEn: a substance added to make food taste stronger
items.example: A flavour enhancer can make soup taste meatier than it is.

items.definitionEn: a protein in wheat and some other grains that some people cannot eat
items.example: Bread without gluten needs a different kind of flour.

items.definitionEn: the natural sugar found in milk
items.example: People who cannot digest lactose often choose oat drinks.

items.definitionEn: having extra vitamins or minerals added
items.example: Some plant drinks are fortified with calcium.

items.definitionEn: milk from which almost all the fat has been removed
items.example: She switched to skimmed milk to cut calories.

items.definitionEn: containing all the natural fat, not reduced
items.example: A pot of full-fat yoghurt tastes creamier than the low-fat sort.

items.definitionEn: no longer safe or pleasant to eat because it is too old
items.example: The milk has gone off — do not pour it on cereal.

items.definitionEn: the last date a perishable food should be eaten for safety
items.example: Chicken must not be cooked after the use-by date.

items.definitionEn: the date until which a food is at its best quality
items.example: Biscuits after the best-before date may taste dull but are often still edible.

items.definitionEn: how long a food stays good to eat under proper storage
items.example: Dried beans have a long shelf life in a cool cupboard.

items.definitionEn: an illness caused by eating contaminated food
items.example: Warm rice left on the table can cause food poisoning.

items.definitionEn: the presence of harmful bacteria or substances in food
items.example: Raw chicken can cause contamination if it touches salad.

items.definitionEn: the spread of harmful bacteria from one food or surface to another
items.example: Use separate boards to avoid cross-contamination.

items.definitionEn: to cook just below boiling point, with small bubbles
items.example: Let the sauce simmer for twenty minutes.

items.definitionEn: to cook food in an oven with fat, often meat or vegetables
items.example: We roast root vegetables with a little oil on Sundays.

items.definitionEn: to change food through the action of yeast or bacteria
items.example: Cabbage can ferment into sauerkraut in a jar.

items.definitionPl: smażyć krótko na małej ilości tłuszczu
items.definitionEn: to fry quickly in a small amount of fat
items.example: Cooks sauté the onions until they turn golden.

items.definitionEn: to cook slowly in liquid; a dish cooked that way
items.example: You can stew cheaper cuts of meat until they soften.

items.definitionEn: to fry food briefly and then cook it slowly in a little liquid
items.example: Chefs braise the beef with stock and onions.

items.definitionPl: gotować w wodzie tuż poniżej wrzenia
items.definitionEn: to cook gently in water or another liquid that is not quite boiling
items.example: You can poach the eggs for three minutes.

items.definitionEn: to put food briefly into boiling water, then often into cold water
items.example: You should blanch the green beans before you freeze them.

items.definitionEn: to preserve food in vinegar or salt water
items.example: They pickle cucumbers every autumn.

items.definitionEn: to preserve meat or fish with salt, smoke or both
items.example: They cure the ham with salt for several weeks.

items.definitionEn: to leave food in a flavoured liquid so it absorbs taste
items.example: You should marinate the tofu for at least an hour.

items.definitionEn: to press and fold dough with your hands
items.example: You must knead the dough until it feels smooth and elastic.

items.definitionEn: to beat eggs or cream quickly until light
items.example: You should whisk the eggs until they look pale and thick.

items.definitionEn: to mix a light ingredient into a heavier one with gentle movements
items.example: Gently fold in the egg whites so the mixture stays airy.

items.definitionEn: to cut cooked meat into slices for serving
items.example: Dad will carve the chicken at the table.

items.definitionEn: to cut or grind meat into very small pieces
items.example: Cooks mince the leftover roast for cottage pie.

items.definitionEn: to pour a thin stream of liquid over food
items.example: Waiters drizzle olive oil over the tomatoes.

items.definitionEn: to cook small pieces of food quickly in a little oil while stirring
items.example: You can stir-fry the vegetables so they stay crisp.

items.definitionEn: to cook food by covering it in hot oil
items.example: If you deep-fry too often, meals become heavy.

items.definitionEn: a dish of meat or vegetables cooked slowly in liquid in the oven
items.example: A winter casserole can feed the whole family.

items.definitionEn: a flavoured liquid made by cooking bones, meat or vegetables in water
items.example: Make stock from leftover bones and vegetables.

items.definitionEn: a sauce made from meat juices, often served with a roast
items.example: Pour gravy over the potatoes, not over the salad.

items.definitionEn: a mixture of flour, egg and liquid used to coat food or make pancakes
items.example: Dip the fish in batter before you fry it.

items.definitionEn: a thick mixture of flour and liquid that is baked
items.example: Leave the dough in a warm place to rise.

items.definitionEn: a microscopic fungus used to make bread rise
items.example: Without yeast the loaf will stay flat.

items.definitionEn: bread made with a fermented starter rather than commercial yeast
items.example: A loaf of sourdough needs time, not just a packet of yeast.

items.definitionEn: to leave dough in a warm place so that it rises before baking
items.example: Cover the tin and prove the dough for forty minutes.

items.definitionEn: to brush food with egg, sugar or jelly so it shines
items.example: Bakers glaze the tart with warmed apricot jam.

items.definitionEn: to heat sugar or vegetables until they brown and sweeten
items.example: Cooks caramelise the onions slowly so they do not burn.

items.definitionEn: to boil a liquid so that some water evaporates and the flavour strengthens
items.example: You should reduce the sauce until it coats the back of a spoon.

items.definitionEn: to make a sauce or soup less watery
items.example: You can thicken the soup with a spoon of mashed potato.

items.definitionEn: to leave a flavouring in a liquid so the taste passes into it
items.example: Cooks infuse the milk with vanilla before they make custard.

items.definitionEn: a way of eating that includes a healthy mix of food groups
items.example: A balanced diet includes vegetables, protein and some wholegrain starch.

items.definitionEn: eating no animal products, including milk, eggs and honey
items.example: The café labels every vegan soup clearly.

items.definitionEn: a person who does not eat meat but does eat fish
items.example: A pescatarian can still order the salmon.

items.definitionEn: a person who mainly eats plant food but occasionally eats meat
items.example: A flexitarian week might include one chicken dinner.

items.definitionEn: difficulty digesting a food, causing discomfort but not a full allergy
items.example: A lactose intolerance is not the same as a milk allergy.

items.definitionEn: a substance in food that the body needs, such as a vitamin or protein
items.example: Spinach provides more than one nutrient, including iron.

items.definitionEn: poor health caused by not having enough of the right foods
items.example: Hidden malnutrition can occur even when calorie intake looks high.

items.definitionEn: not getting enough food or nutrients to stay healthy
items.example: An undernourished child may feel tired in every lesson.

items.definitionEn: the state of having so much body fat that it harms health
items.example: Childhood obesity is discussed in biology and in form time.

items.definitionEn: the amount of energy you get from food and drink
items.example: Athletes raise their calorie intake during hard training.

items.definitionEn: energy from food that offers little nutritional value
items.example: Fizzy drinks are a classic source of empty calories.

items.definitionEn: a very strict, short-term eating plan that cuts food severely
items.example: A crash diet often fails as soon as ordinary meals return.

items.definitionEn: a fashionable eating plan that promises fast results with little evidence
items.example: A fad diet that bans whole food groups is rarely sustainable.

items.definitionEn: repeatedly losing weight and then gaining it again
items.example: Repeated yo-yo dieting can leave people tired and discouraged.

items.definitionEn: choosing sensible amounts of food rather than eating until the plate is empty
items.example: Good portion control is easier if you use a smaller plate.

items.definitionEn: going without food for a set time, often for health or religion
items.example: Medical advice should come before fasting for several days.

items.definitionEn: an eating pattern with regular periods of not eating
items.example: Doctors say intermittent fasting does not suit everyone, especially teenagers.

items.definitionEn: a pill or powder taken to add nutrients to your diet
items.example: A supplement cannot replace vegetables and sleep.

items.definitionEn: a substance in some foods thought to protect cells from damage
items.example: Berries are often mentioned as a source of antioxidant compounds.

items.definitionEn: a food or drink containing live bacteria that may help the gut
items.example: A probiotic yoghurt is not a cure for every stomach ache.

items.definitionEn: the amount of liquid you drink
items.example: Doctors remind patients to increase fluid intake during a fever.

items.definitionEn: lacking enough water in the body
items.example: After the match he felt dizzy and dehydrated.

items.definitionEn: made mainly or entirely from plants rather than animals
items.example: A plant-based burger should still list its ingredients clearly.

items.definitionEn: containing no milk or products made from milk
items.example: The muffin is dairy-free but it still contains eggs.

items.definitionEn: containing a large amount of protein
items.example: A high-protein breakfast can be eggs on wholegrain toast.

items.definitionEn: containing little starch or sugar
items.example: A low-carb supper might skip the rice and add extra salad.

items.definitionEn: containing no added sugar
items.example: A packet of sugar-free gum is not a substitute for brushing your teeth.

items.definitionEn: food that is as close as possible to its natural state
items.example: A wholefood lunch might be beans, rice and raw vegetables.

items.definitionEn: a serious mental health condition involving harmful eating patterns
items.example: If you worry about an eating disorder, speak to a doctor or a trusted adult.

items.definitionEn: an episode of eating a very large amount of food in a short time
items.example: A leaflet may mention a binge as one sign of an eating disorder.

items.definitionEn: food you eat because it makes you feel emotionally better
items.example: Toast and soup is comfort food on a grey afternoon.

items.definitionEn: eating in response to feelings rather than hunger
items.example: Late-night emotional eating after an argument does not solve the argument.

items.definitionEn: a person who is very interested in cooking and trying dishes
items.example: A foodie will queue for a new bakery without complaining.

items.definitionEn: connected with high-quality, carefully prepared food
items.example: A gourmet menu can still start with a simple seasonal soup.

items.definitionEn: a person who advises on food and nutrients, not always a regulated doctor
items.example: Ask whether the nutritionist has recognised qualifications.

items.definitionEn: a qualified health professional who gives evidence-based diet advice
items.example: A hospital dietitian can plan meals after an operation.

items.definitionEn: a person who refuses many foods and accepts only a few
items.example: A fussy eater may still learn to like new flavours slowly.

items.definitionEn: extra money left for waiting staff for their service
items.example: In Britain people often leave a ten percent tip.

items.definitionEn: an arrangement to have a table kept for you at a set time
items.example: Friday night requires a reservation at that bistro.

items.definitionEn: a mark of excellence given to a restaurant by the Michelin guide
items.example: The bistro earned a Michelin star for its seasonal cooking.

items.definitionEn: ordered as individual dishes from a menu, not as a fixed set
items.example: I ordered à la carte rather than the set lunch.

items.definitionEn: a limited list of dishes offered at a fixed price
items.example: The weekday set menu is cheaper than ordering separately.

items.definitionEn: a sequence of small dishes chosen by the chef
items.example: A tasting menu can last two hours and many courses.

items.definitionEn: a restaurant specialist who advises on wine
items.example: Ask the sommelier if you do not know the wine list.

items.definitionEn: an extra percentage added to a restaurant bill for staff
items.example: Check whether a service charge is already included.

items.definitionEn: a fixed fee some restaurants add per person before food
items.example: The cover charge paid for bread and olives.

items.definitionEn: the polite way of eating and behaving during a meal
items.example: Good table manners include not talking with your mouth full.

items.definitionEn: a drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite
items.example: They offered a small aperitif while we read the menu.

items.definitionEn: a mixed drink without alcohol
items.example: She ordered a mocktail so she could drive home.

items.definitionEn: having no free tables left
items.example: The restaurant was fully booked until half past nine.

items.definitionEn: a customer who arrives without a reservation
items.example: A walk-in might still get a seat at the bar.

items.definitionEn: formal, high-quality restaurant food and service
items.example: A night of fine dining is a rare treat, not a weekly habit.

items.definitionEn: ready-to-eat food sold from stalls or carts
items.example: The street food at the market included falafel and warm pretzels.

items.definitionEn: a vehicle from which cooked food is sold
items.example: The food truck sells grilled cheese at lunchtime.

items.definitionEn: a large plate of food designed for several people to share
items.example: We ordered a sharing platter instead of three starters.

items.definitionEn: costing more than it is worth
items.example: The mineral water was overpriced for a small bottle.

items.definitionEn: worth the price you pay because of quality or quantity
items.example: The lunch deal offers real value for money.

items.definitionEn: a journalist who reviews restaurants and dishes
items.example: A food critic should pay the bill like any other guest.

items.definitionEn: the recipe a cook or restaurant is best known for
items.example: The signature dish is beetroot risotto with goat's cheese.

items.definitionEn: a dish recommended or created by the chef that day
items.example: Ask what the chef's special is before you order.

items.definitionEn: a need to avoid or include certain foods for health or belief
items.example: Tell the waiter about any dietary requirement when you book.

items.definitionEn: a substance that can cause an allergic reaction
items.example: Menus must highlight a major allergen such as peanuts.

items.definitionEn: prepared according to Islamic rules, especially of meat
items.example: The canteen offers a halal chicken option.

items.definitionEn: prepared according to Jewish dietary law
items.example: A kosher kitchen keeps meat and dairy strictly apart.

items.definitionEn: a fee for bringing your own wine into a restaurant
items.example: The corkage was ten pounds per bottle.

items.definitionEn: the restaurant's ordinary, usually cheaper wine
items.example: A glass of house wine was enough with the pasta.

items.definitionEn: food that has been changed from its natural state, often with additives
items.example: A diet of processed food tends to be high in salt and sugar.

items.definitionEn: edible food that is thrown away instead of being eaten
items.example: Planning meals is a simple way to cut food waste.

items.definitionEn: produced without synthetic pesticides or fertilisers
items.example: Some organic vegetables cost more but shoppers still choose them.

items.definitionEn: a system that aims to pay producers in poorer countries a fairer price
items.example: I buy fair trade coffee to support the growers.

items.definitionEn: reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
items.example: Droughts threaten food security in several regions.

items.definitionEn: the distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
items.example: Local apples have fewer food miles than fruit flown in winter.

items.definitionEn: keeping large numbers of animals in intensive conditions for cheap meat or eggs
items.example: Many consumers now question factory farming.

items.definitionEn: food served soon after it is grown, with few middlemen
items.example: The bistro advertises a farm-to-table menu in summer.

items.definitionEn: keeping hens in small cages to produce eggs cheaply
items.example: The law restricts battery farming of hens in the United Kingdom.

items.definitionEn: allowed to move outdoors, especially of hens or their eggs
items.example: She pays extra for free-range eggs.

items.definitionEn: the health and living conditions of animals kept by humans
items.example: Labels now mention animal welfare more often than ten years ago.

items.definitionEn: farm animals such as cattle, sheep and pigs
items.example: The farm keeps livestock on the higher fields.

items.definitionEn: having genes changed in a laboratory to give a plant or animal new traits
items.example: Some shoppers avoid genetically modified soya.

items.definitionEn: a substance put in food to colour, preserve or flavour it
items.example: Some people avoid products with a long list of food additive codes.

items.definitionPl: superżywność (modny produkt o wysokiej wartości odżywczej)
items.definitionEn: a food marketed as especially rich in nutrients
items.example: Blueberries are often labelled a superfood in magazine articles.

items.definitionEn: growing food in a way that can continue without ruining soil, water or wildlife
items.example: Supporters of sustainable farming try to protect the land for the next harvest.

items.definitionEn: fish caught or farmed in a way that does not empty the oceans
items.example: The restaurant switched to sustainable seafood certified by a label.

items.definitionEn: fruit and vegetables harvested at the natural time of year
items.example: A market stall full of seasonal produce is cheaper in autumn.

items.definitionPl: pochodzący z lokalnych upraw lub hodowli
items.definitionEn: obtained from nearby farms or producers
items.example: The menu says the cheese is locally sourced.

items.definitionEn: the information printed on packaging about ingredients and nutrition
items.example: Clear food labelling helps people with allergies.

items.definitionEn: the ability to follow a food back to where it was produced
items.example: Good traceability matters when a batch has to be withdrawn.

items.definitionEn: the sequence of steps that takes food from farm to shop
items.example: A broken supply chain can empty supermarket shelves.

items.definitionEn: a company that owns many large food shops
items.example: A supermarket chain can push prices down for farmers.

items.definitionEn: a situation in which there is not enough food available
items.example: Floods caused a food shortage of fresh vegetables.

items.definitionPl: obszar bez dostępu do zdrowej żywności
items.definitionEn: a neighbourhood with few shops selling fresh, healthy food
items.example: Living in a food desert makes a balanced diet more expensive.

items.definitionEn: a charity that gives donated food to people who cannot afford it
items.example: The food bank needs tins and long-life milk this month.

items.definitionEn: not being able to afford enough healthy food
items.example: Hidden food poverty can exist next door to a full supermarket.

items.definitionEn: made mostly from industrial ingredients rather than whole foods
items.example: An ultra-processed snack often lists a dozen additives.

items.definitionEn: food that is quick to prepare, often packaged or ready-made
items.example: A frozen convenience food helps on late nights, but not every night.

items.definitionEn: a complete dish sold cooked, which you only need to heat
items.example: A ready meal is useful when the cooker is broken.

items.definitionEn: an industrial fat, now widely restricted, that harms heart health
items.example: Many countries have banned trans fat in supermarket food.

items.definitionEn: a fatty substance in blood; some foods can affect its level
items.example: Eggs are no longer treated as a simple cholesterol villain.

items.definitionEn: a government charge on drinks with a lot of added sugar
items.example: The sugar tax pushed some brands to use less sugar.

items.definitionEn: wrapping that can break down into soil in a compost bin
items.example: The takeaway switched to compostable packaging last year.

items.definitionEn: a chemical used instead of sugar to make food taste sweet
items.example: An artificial sweetener can leave a bitter aftertaste.
